title: OpenAI's Decisions API moves from limited preview to public beta
subtitle: The classification-focused endpoint built on GPT-6 Luna returns answers in 150 milliseconds and is now open to all developers — up from the invite-only preview announced at DevDay.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI opened the Decisions API to all developers in public beta this week, roughly eight days after unveiling it in limited preview at its September 29 DevDay. The endpoint is built on a specialized version of GPT-6 Luna and does one narrow job: it picks between a finite set of answers that the developer defines in advance, returning each choice as a probability score rather than a block of text. OpenAI says it returns classified answers in 150 milliseconds versus the roughly 1.6 seconds a standard call to Luna takes through the Responses API — about ten times faster for the same decision.

The design is explicit about what it is for. Developers hand Decisions a question, a list of allowed answers, and context in text or images. The API returns a ranked distribution across the allowed answers. That shape is useful for a specific pattern that has quietly become the backbone of agent systems: routing. An agent that decides which tool to call, a moderation pipeline that classifies content, a support assistant that picks which playbook to follow — these are all decisions-shaped tasks that previously ran through full chat completions and paid the latency and cost of generating text that nobody read. Decisions skips the text generation step entirely.

The commercial pitch is a direct shot at Jev and similar routing-specific services that have taken share from OpenAI inside agent stacks over the past year. Price per call, maximum answer-set size, and fine-tuning support are still not disclosed in the beta documentation, which is the kind of gap that keeps enterprise architects nervous even when the latency numbers look good. OpenAI says it will share pricing details at the broader rollout. The company has also not published independent evaluations of accuracy against generative Luna for the same classification tasks — reviewers who got early access report it holds up on simple routing but degrades on long, ambiguous categorizations.

A takeaway for learners: when a provider ships a cheaper, faster endpoint for one narrow task, treat it as a sign that the task has stabilized. Classification and routing are no longer research problems — they are commodity primitives. If you are building anything agentic, read Decisions' docs, Jev's docs, and the Anthropic classification API docs side by side. The pattern they share is more durable than any one vendor's marketing: fast, probabilistic choice over a bounded set is a layer in modern AI systems you will keep using for years.
